text:
The brightest flames, they say, burn just before going out. The autumn leaves blanketing the mountains in red seemed to be burning with equal intensity, as if sensing the end of their season. By mid-November, the foliage in Naeseorak, the western side of Daecheongbong Peak, had largely faded and fallen, but Oeseorak was still displaying its final burst of color.
Even beneath thick fog that limited visibility, the mountains' beauty was impossible to conceal. Peaks emerged through the mist, overlooking forests ablaze with autumn hues. In late fall, Mount Seorak remains beautiful enough to delight even visitors who arrive a little late for the foliage season.
Word of its spectacular scenery has crossed oceans. Mount Seorak's autumn foliage is now as well-known overseas as it is in Korea. Foreign tourists have long been discovering the country's mountains, and their travels have expanded beyond Seoul and Jeju Island to the mountainous regions of Gangwon Province. This fall, foreign guests accounted for 50 percent of all visitors staying at Kensington Hotel Seorak, located within Seoraksan National Park, up from just 22 percent in 2024.
A French family visiting Mount Seorak was particularly impressed.
"We come from Chamonix, a village where Mont Blanc (4,807 meters) is practically our backyard mountain, but the autumn foliage we saw today at Mount Seorak is unforgettable," they said.
"Being surrounded by mountain ranges covered in autumn colors feels like stepping into a fortress of fall. It's a landscape you can't even find in the Alps," they added.
Oeseorak is the area that typically comes to mind when Koreans think of school field trips to Mount Seorak. Centered around Seorak-dong, it was once a must-visit destination for students, with Biryong Falls, Biseondae Rock and Heundeulbawi Rock among the standard stops. After substantial rainfall, visitors may also be lucky enough to see Towangseong Falls, whose 320-meter cascade is the longest in Korea. Normally difficult to see, the waterfall's three-tiered cascade comes fully into view only after heavy rain.
Seorak-dong enjoyed its heyday in the 1970s and 1980s. In 1969, then-President Park Chung-hee was impressed by Yosemite National Park in the United States and ordered the development of a concentrated district for accommodation and commercial facilities. The complex was completed in 1978, and by the 1980s, school groups from across the country were flocking to the area. In 1995, Mount Seorak attracted 5.18 million visitors.
Its decline began in the 1990s, as overseas travel became more accessible and modern resorts opened in downtown Sokcho. Today, roughly two out of every three lodging establishments and restaurants in the area have closed, leaving only a handful of businesses, including Kensington Hotel Seorak, still operating. The growing number of international visitors is therefore especially welcome.
Autumn foliage is undoubtedly the biggest draw for foreign tourists. During October and November, Mount Seorak attracts almost as many international visitors as Seoul.
Anise, 28, a French visitor making her third trip to the mountain, said she had never seen such vivid shades of red and yellow in the forests of southern France.
"I really love the contrast between the green, red and yellow," she said.
Although autumn foliage can also be sen in Europe, the variety of tree species is more limited, and intensely red leaves are particularly uncommon compared with those in Korea. Of the approximately 290 tree species that produce red autumn foliage, more than 152 are native to East Asia, while only 24 are native to Europe. Perhaps for this reason, Mount Seorak sees a particularly notable number of visitors making the long journey from Europe during foliage season.
Another advantage for visitors is that the peak foliage season differs between Naeseorak and Oeseorak, despite both being part of the same mountain range.
Fritz, 29, who traveled from Belgium, said nature, particularly the autumn foliage, was Mount Seorak's greatest attraction.
"I knew I was arriving just after the peak foliage season, but this side of the mountain (Oeseorak) is still incredibly beautiful," he said.
Experienced hikers also appreciate the mountain's rugged terrain. Even Fritz, who enjoys hiking in the Alps, found Mount Seorak challenging. He completed the Dinosaur Ridge, a demanding mountain trail, over seven and a half hours.
"It was difficult because you have to gain a lot of elevation in a short amount of time, but every time I climbed higher, another spectacular view opened up," he said. "The scenery was breathtaking throughout the route, as the trail repeatedly descended and climbed along the ridge."
He was also struck by Mount Seorak's granite formations, which looked quite different from the mountains of Europe, despite granite being a familiar rock type there.
"It's not marble, but it has the same kind of beauty as marble," he said.
The most popular hiking route among visitors is, unsurprisingly, the Ulsanbawi Rock trail. Starting at the small park entrance in Seorak-dong, the 3.8-kilometer one-way route passes Sinheungsa Temple and Heundeulbawi Rock before reaching Ulsanbawi. The hike takes approximately two hours. Most of the more than 10 foreign tourists interviewed by this reporter had completed the course.
Foreign visitors who were less accustomed to hiking praised the well-maintained trails. For the French family from Chamonix, only the father was an experienced hiker, while the mother and daughter were beginners. The accessible trails nevertheless allowed the entire family to enjoy the hike together.
Visitors can also take a cable car to Gwongeumseong Fortress, making the ascent considerably easier. The ride takes just five minutes to reach the upper station at an elevation of 699 meters. A short climb along a rocky path leads to the fortress's beacon tower.
On clear days, visitors can take in panoramic views of Ulsanbawi Rock, Oeseorak's granite peaks, downtown Sokcho and the East Sea. A light layer of fog can make the landscape even more mysterious, creating the sensation of standing above the clouds.
Seoraksan National Park has another unusual attraction: Kensington Hotel Seorak.
Its exterior resembles an aging condominium complex, but the interior has been meticulously renovated in a classic British style. After acquiring the property in 1996, E-Land transformed it around a British royal theme. A double-decker bus that once operated on the streets of London in the 1950s now stands outside the main entrance.
The lobby, restaurants and guest room corridors are filled with unexpected historical artifacts. Among them are an arrow pierced by another arrow, fired by archer Kim Soo-nyung when she repeatedly hit the exact center of the target at the 1988 Seoul Olympics; a guitar bearing the handwritten signatures of all four Beatles members; a suit once worn by John Lennon; and the coronation mace of King Edward VII of Britain.
The items, many of which would be worthy of display in a museum, were either donated by prominent figures or acquired at auctions by E-Land Group Chairman Park Sung-soo.
The hotel's own history is equally intriguing. According to the hotel, Park ordered its construction so he could use a suite as a private retreat. That history explains why the hotel was built so close to Mount Seorak, on land within the national park — something that would be difficult to permit today.
The hotel's presidential suite retains details from that era, including the phoenix motif on its door. An additional partition door blocks off several ordinary guest rooms adjoining the suite. When the president stayed there, the arrangement prevented members of the public from entering the area while providing accommodation for his entourage.
The corridor divides the suite into a reception room and a bedroom on opposite sides. In reality, the reception room is on the left and the bedroom on the right, but the original architectural plans deliberately reversed the arrangement for security reasons.
